latest.comment: Daniel’s poem turns on a deceptively large claim: that a dog’s look can meet a human look as something like recognition, not mere stimulus-response. That hinge—mutual gaze—quietly imports a whole philosophy of encounter. Read through Martin Buber, the poem stages a brief “I–Thou” moment in the middle of city throughput: the avenue is a corridor of motion until the reciprocal glance makes a relationship, however fleeting, appear. Yet because Daniel gives us no other cue—no leash, no owner, no breed, no context—the poem also risks smuggling in anthropomorphism as an unexamined default: the dog “turned to look at me” can be read as fellowship, but it can just as plausibly be vigilance, training, hunger, or a thousand other non-human motives. That ambiguity is where the poem could press harder. Derrida (in The Animal That Therefore I Am) lingers on the unease of being seen by an animal, not because the animal becomes human, but because the human loses the comfort of being the only subject in the scene. Daniel gestures toward that unsettling reversal—“I turned… / The dog turned…”—but stops just before asking what, exactly, shifts in the speaker when the city’s ordinary hierarchy of observer and observed collapses for an instant. If the poem’s aim is simplicity, it achieves it; if its aim is insight, the missed opportunity is to let the mutual look do more than mirror the lines—to let it disturb the speaker’s certainty about what kind of “meeting” this is.
